questions.statement: Choose the relative clause that defines a specific person.
questions.context: You want to identify one specific person in a crowd.

options.text: The student who lives next door is my cousin.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Who' is the relative pronoun for people, and a defining clause narrows the reference to one particular student.

options.text: The student what lives next door is my cousin.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What' cannot function as a relative pronoun referring to a person followed by a clause.

options.text: The student which lives next door is my cousin.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Which' is used for things, not for people, in defining relative clauses.

options.text: The student lives next door is my cousin.
options.feedback: Wrong. Without a relative pronoun the two verbs clash and the sentence is ungrammatical.

questions.explanation:
A defining relative clause uses who, which or that and narrows the noun it follows to a specific individual or item.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the relative clause that correctly refers to a thing.
questions.context: You describe a thing, not a person.

options.text: The book who I borrowed is overdue.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Who' refers to people and cannot modify the noun 'book'.

options.text: The book which I borrowed is overdue.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Which' is the standard relative pronoun for objects or things.

options.text: The book whom I borrowed is overdue.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Whom' is used for people as the object of a preposition, not for things.

options.text: The book what I borrowed is overdue.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What' cannot be the object of a preposition in a relative clause like this.

questions.explanation:
Relative pronouns carry meaning: who and whom for people, which for things and that for either in defining clauses.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the non-defining relative clause.
questions.context: The relative clause must be set off with commas because the information is extra.

options.text: My brother, that lives in Arequipa, is visiting next week.
options.feedback: Wrong. Non-defining clauses in formal English use who or which, not that.

options.text: My brother lives in Arequipa is visiting next week.
options.feedback: Wrong. Without commas the clause would be read as defining, and the sentence as written lacks the punctuation that separates it.

options.text: My brother, who lives in Arequipa, is visiting next week.
options.feedback: Correct. Commas and non-defining who signal that the clause adds extra information about an already identified person.

options.text: My brother lives in Arequipa, is visiting next week.
options.feedback: Wrong. The punctuation is misplaced and the sentence has two finite verbs with no relative structure.

questions.explanation:
A non-defining clause adds supplementary information about something already identified, and it is set off with commas.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence with the correct relative pronoun.
questions.context: The pronoun case depends on its role inside the clause.

options.text: The teacher what I spoke was very patient.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What' cannot serve as the object of a preposition.

options.text: The teacher which I spoke was very patient.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Which' refers to things and cannot refer to a teacher.

options.text: The teacher who I spoke was very patient.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Who' is the subject form and cannot follow a preposition in this position.

options.text: The teacher to whom I spoke was very patient.
options.feedback: Correct. After the preposition 'to' the object form 'whom' is required in formal written English.

questions.explanation:
A relative pronoun takes the case of its function within the clause, so after a preposition the object form is required.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the relative pronoun is the object and can be omitted.
questions.context: The sentence must contain a relative clause in the object position.

options.text: The essay she wrote won a prize.
options.feedback: Correct. 'She' is the object of 'wrote' inside the clause, so the pronoun has been left out, which is standard English.

options.text: The essay whom wrote won a prize.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Whom wrote' places the object form in the subject position, which is not correct.

options.text: The essay who wrote won a prize.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Who' refers to a person and cannot modify the noun 'essay'.

options.text: The essay wrote she won a prize.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Wrote she' reverses the normal word order and does not form a clause.

questions.explanation:
When the relative pronoun is the object of the clause, its omission is possible and common, especially in everyday speech.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the statement that best explains the difference between the two types.
questions.context: A grammarian compares defining and non-defining clauses.

options.text: A defining clause always requires commas, while a non-defining clause never uses them.
options.feedback: Wrong. It reverses the punctuation rule, since defining clauses are not normally set off with commas.

options.text: A defining clause narrows the reference of the noun, while a non-defining clause adds information about an already identified noun.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the defining functional difference, and it explains the different punctuation each type requires.

options.text: A defining clause must contain a verb, while a non-defining clause may not contain one.
options.feedback: Wrong. Both types contain finite verbs, since they are clauses rather than phrases.

options.text: A defining clause can only modify people, while a non-defining clause can only modify things.
options.feedback: Wrong. Both types can modify either people or things; the choice of pronoun does not depend on that.

questions.explanation:
The distinction between the two types is about information, not about the kind of noun or the presence of a verb.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the version in which the punctuation matches the type of clause used.
questions.context: An editor checks a sentence for an unnecessary comma.

options.text: The professor, who wrote three books is retiring.
options.feedback: Wrong. The opening comma has no matching closing comma, so the punctuation is inconsistent.

options.text: The professor who wrote three books, is retiring.
options.feedback: Wrong. The commas in this version make the clause non-defining, which contradicts the sense of a single identified professor.

options.text: The professor, who wrote three books, is retiring.
options.feedback: Correct. This version uses no commas, so the clause is read as defining and restricts the reference to one specific professor.

options.text: The professor who wrote three books is retiring.
options.feedback: Wrong. The commas here make the clause non-defining, which restricts rather than explains, so the sense changes.

questions.explanation:
Punctuation is the visible marker of clause type, and moving or removing a comma changes which reading the sentence supports.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the relative clause that correctly modifies a time expression.
questions.context: A sentence needs a clause modifying a time expression.

options.text: On the days when the market opens early the prices, fall.
options.feedback: Wrong. The comma is misplaced in front of the main verb, which breaks the sentence structure.

options.text: On the days that the market opens early, the prices fall.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'That' can introduce a clause but 'on the days that the market opens early' is less idiomatic than 'when'.

options.text: On the days which the market opens early, the prices fall.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Which' would require an object role and cannot introduce this adverbial clause about time.

options.text: On the days when the market opens early, the prices fall.
options.feedback: Correct. 'When' introduces a clause of time and is the natural connective after 'on the days'.

questions.explanation:
Time expressions are commonly extended with a when-clause, and when is the connective that fits this pattern naturally.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence with the correct relative pronoun after a preposition.
questions.context: A description needs a clause referring to a person with a preposition.

options.text: The colleague with whom I share an office is on leave.
options.feedback: Correct. The pronoun is the object of the preposition 'with', so the form 'whom' is required.

options.text: The colleague with what I share an office is on leave.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What' cannot be the object of a preposition in a relative clause.

options.text: The colleague with which I share an office is on leave.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Which' refers to things and cannot stand for a colleague.

options.text: The colleague with who I share an office is on leave.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Who' is the subject form and does not follow a preposition here.

questions.explanation:
Formal English requires whom for the object of a preposition, and this rule is frequently tested in written examinations.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses a relative pronoun to refer to two things.
questions.context: A sentence needs two items described in one clause.

options.text: The bag and the umbrella which I bought are wet.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Which' cannot stand for a plural combination of two different nouns in a defining clause.

options.text: The bag and the umbrella that I bought are wet.
options.feedback: Correct. 'That' is the only relative pronoun that can refer to two nouns joined by and in a defining clause.

options.text: The bag and the umbrella whom I bought are wet.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Whom' refers to people, so it cannot modify a bag and an umbrella.

options.text: The bag and the umbrella what I bought are wet.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What' cannot refer back to two nouns as a subject pronoun here.

questions.explanation:
That has a special use with two nouns joined by and, which is why it is the only workable pronoun in this sentence.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the definition that follows the style rule.
questions.context: A definition style guide discourages using a pronoun to refer to people.

options.text: A user is a person which has an account.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Which' cannot refer to a person.

options.text: A user is a person that has an account.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'That' is grammatical in defining clauses but is avoided in careful style guides when it refers to people.

options.text: A user is a person who has an account.
options.feedback: Correct. Using who rather than that respects people and is the convention preferred in formal definition writing.

options.text: A user is a person what has an account.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What' cannot function as a relative pronoun referring back to a person in a definition.

questions.explanation:
Where both who and that are grammatically possible, style guides usually recommend who because it avoids the impersonal feel of that.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly expresses possession within a relative clause.
questions.context: An exercise tests relative clauses with a possessive relationship.

options.text: The author which novels I admire most was born in Arequipa.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Which' has no possessive form and refers to things without indicating ownership.

options.text: The author whom novels I admire most was born in Arequipa.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Whom' is an object form and has no possessive function.

options.text: The author who's novels I admire most was born in Arequipa.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Who's' is the contraction of 'who is' and cannot express possession.

options.text: The author whose novels I admire most was born in Arequipa.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Whose' expresses possession and is the only relative pronoun able to do so.

questions.explanation:
Possession inside a relative clause requires whose, which is why the possessive relative pronoun is a standard test item.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly shares a verb across two subjects.
questions.context: A report describes two people using one verb.

options.text: My father and my uncle were both born in the provinces.
options.feedback: Correct. With two subjects joined by and, the plural auxiliary 'were' is required and both verbs appear once as 'were born'.

options.text: My father and my uncle both born in the provinces.
options.feedback: Wrong. A finite verb is missing, so the sentence has no structure.

options.text: My father and my uncle were both born in the provinces is true.
options.feedback: Wrong. The verb phrase is complete and cannot be followed by 'is true'.

options.text: My father and my uncle was both born in the provinces.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was' agrees with a singular subject, but the subject here is a plural pair.

questions.explanation:
A relative clause can stretch across two coordinated subjects, but the number agreement is decided by both subjects together.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the version that correctly separates extra information with a non-defining clause.
questions.context: An editor rewrites a long sentence using a non-defining clause.

options.text: Cusco which lies in the south-east of Peru has a large cathedral.
options.feedback: Wrong. Without commas the clause would restrict the reference, which is not the intended meaning.

options.text: Cusco, which lies in the south-east of Peru, has a large cathedral.
options.feedback: Correct. Commas plus non-defining which correctly present the location as additional information about the city.

options.text: Cusco, which lies the south-east of Peru, has a large cathedral.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Which lies the south-east' lacks the preposition 'in' that the phrase requires.

options.text: Cusco, that lies in the south-east of Peru, has a large cathedral.
options.feedback: Wrong. Non-defining clauses in formal English do not use that.

questions.explanation:
When the extra information concerns a thing rather than a person, non-defining clauses use which, and the commas must be balanced.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the pair in which both pronouns are used correctly.
questions.context: A grammar task tests the distinction between who and whom.

options.text: The man who called me left a message. / The man to who I spoke was helpful.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'To who' uses the subject form after a preposition, which is informal at best and wrong in formal writing.

options.text: The man whom called me left a message. / The man who I spoke was helpful.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Whom called' puts the object form in the subject position, and 'who I spoke' follows a preposition.

options.text: The man who called me left a message. / The man to whom I spoke was helpful.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Who' is the subject of 'called' and 'whom' is the object of the preposition 'to', so both are right.

options.text: The man whom called me left a message. / The man to whom I spoke was helpful.
options.feedback: Wrong. The first clause misuses whom as a subject, even though the second one is correct.

questions.explanation:
Case in relative pronouns depends on the role inside the clause: subject position takes who or that and object position takes whom.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which both relative clauses are correctly formed.
questions.context: An exam tests a sentence with two different relative clauses.

options.text: The car what she bought from the dealer whom offered a discount was expensive.
options.feedback: Wrong. Both pronouns are wrong: 'what' cannot be the object and 'whom' cannot be the subject.

options.text: The car that she bought from the dealer whom offered a discount was expensive.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Whom' is the object form and cannot serve as the subject of 'offered'.

options.text: The car what she bought from the dealer who offered a discount was expensive.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What' cannot be used as an object relative pronoun in a defining clause.

options.text: The car that she bought from the dealer who offered a discount was expensive.
options.feedback: Correct. 'That' defines the car as the object of 'bought' and 'who' is the subject of 'offered', so both clauses are correct.

questions.explanation:
A single sentence can carry several relative clauses, and each one must be judged separately for pronoun choice and case.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence conveys the most information with the fewest words?
questions.context: A stylometry exercise evaluates sentences for information density.

options.text: The 1998 report that the team wrote in Lima won an award.
options.feedback: Correct. Omitting the object relative pronoun gives the same meaning with fewer words, which is the most economical version.

options.text: The 1998 report what the team wrote in Lima won an award.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What' is incorrect here, so this version is not an option in any case.

options.text: The 1998 report the team wrote in Lima won an award.
options.feedback: Wrong. Including 'that' is correct style but adds a word unnecessarily when the pronoun can be omitted.

options.text: The 1998 report which the team wrote in Lima won an award.
options.feedback: Wrong. Using 'which' is grammatical but adds a word that the object position allows us to leave out.

questions.explanation:
Economy in writing comes from omitting relative pronouns that the grammar allows to be left out, especially in the object position.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the explanation that accounts for the sentence 'The reason he was late was the traffic.'
questions.context: A grammar exercise examines a verb whose clause is missing a relative pronoun.

options.text: The sentence is missing the relative pronoun 'that' and is therefore ungrammatical.
options.feedback: Wrong. The omission is permitted because the pronoun is the object of the preposition implied by the noun.

options.text: The relative pronoun is the object of the noun 'reason', so it can be omitted without loss of meaning.
options.feedback: Correct. The clause 'he was late' is a complement of 'reason', so the relative pronoun may be omitted.

options.text: The relative pronoun is the subject of the clause and must appear at the start.
options.feedback: Wrong. The pronoun here is not the subject of the clause, which is headed by 'he'.

options.text: The relative pronoun must be 'which' because 'reason' refers to an idea rather than a person.
options.feedback: Wrong. The choice of pronoun depends on whether the referent is a person or a thing, not on whether it is abstract.

questions.explanation:
Nouns such as reason, fact and news take a clause as a complement, and the relative pronoun in that position is always omissible.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses what to refer to a previous idea.
questions.context: An exam item tests relative clauses that refer to whole clauses.

options.text: He missed the last bus, that made him miss the interview.
options.feedback: Wrong. Non-defining clauses about ideas use which, not that.

options.text: He missed the last bus, what made him miss the interview.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What' cannot be used as a relative pronoun referring back to a whole clause in this way.

options.text: He missed the last bus, which made him miss the interview.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Which' can refer to an entire preceding clause as well as to a single noun, which is its distinctive capacity.

options.text: He missed the last bus, whom made him miss the interview.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Whom' refers to people and cannot modify a preceding clause.

questions.explanation:
A relative pronoun that can stand for a whole clause, such as which, is far more flexible than one that must refer to a single noun.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the verb inside the relative clause agrees correctly.
questions.context: A grammar task tests the number agreement inside a relative clause.

options.text: The list of names which are published yesterday is now online.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are published yesterday' is not a valid combination of tense and time expression.

options.text: The list of names that were published yesterday are now online.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are' would also have to refer to the plural 'names', but the subject of the main clause is the singular 'list'.

options.text: The list of names that was published yesterday is now online.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Were' would be required if the clause modified the plural 'names' rather than the singular 'list'.

options.text: The list of names that were published yesterday is now online.
options.feedback: Correct. The noun that the clause modifies is 'list', which is singular, so 'was' inside the clause is correct.

questions.explanation: A verb inside a relative clause agrees with the noun immediately preceding the relative pronoun, not necessarily with the subject of the whole sentence.
questions.subject: ingles
